title: India Defeats Pakistan at Asian Games Amid No‑Handshake Protocol and Delayed Ceremony
body:
India clinched the Asian Games cricket gold on Sunday, edging out arch‑rivals Pakistan by 19 runs in a tightly contested final at Nagoya’s Mizuho Park Ground. The hosts, who posted a formidable 211 for six, were unable to chase down the target despite a spirited 96‑run knock from Pakistan’s Hasan Nawaz, leaving the Indian side to celebrate a historic triumph in a match played without the usual post‑match handshakes and with a brief ceremony delay caused by technical glitches.

The final was a showcase of the growing stature of cricket within the multi‑sport Asian Games framework. India, the reigning T20 World Cup champions, entered the tournament as clear favourites, yet the path to the gold was far from straightforward. After a dominant group‑stage performance, the Indian side faced a resilient Pakistani unit in the knockout stage, setting the stage for a classic sub‑continental showdown that captivated the modest but vocal crowd in Nagoya. The atmosphere was electric, with chants echoing across the stadium each time a boundary was struck, underscoring the deep-rooted rivalry that extends beyond sport.

India’s innings was anchored by a composed 71 from captain Ruturaj Gaikwad, who combined aggression with prudence to steady the ship after early wickets fell. Middle‑order contributions from Shubman Gill (45) and the explosive finish from Hardik Pandya, who smashed 32 off 18 balls, propelled the total beyond 200—a benchmark that historically proves decisive in limited‑overs cricket. The decision to bat first, influenced by a slight overcast and a damp outfield, paid dividends as the pitch offered a balanced contest between bat and ball, allowing India to set a target that tested Pakistan’s chase.

Pakistan’s reply began brightly, with openers opening aggressively and establishing a 70‑run partnership. However, a decisive spell from India’s spin duo—Rashid Khan and Yuzvendra Chahal—turned the tide, extracting turn and bounce that troubled the Pakistani batsmen. The turning point arrived when Nawaz, who had been the tournament’s top scorer, arrived at the crease with the team needing 140 runs from 20 overs. His 96‑run effort, marked by deft timing and a series of powerful drives, kept Pakistan within reach, but a late‑innings wobble—three wickets falling for just 12 runs—saw the required run rate surge beyond 10 per over. The final overs saw India’s fielders tighten their grip, and a crucial run‑out of Nawaz’s partner sealed the match.

Beyond the on‑field drama, the final highlighted logistical challenges that sometimes accompany emerging sports events. A brief delay in the medal ceremony, caused by a technical fault in the podium’s electronic display, forced officials to pause before presenting the gold medals. While the interruption was minor, it underscored the need for robust infrastructure as cricket continues to integrate into larger multi‑sport platforms. Additionally, the absence of the customary handshake ceremony—mandated by health protocols—was noted by players and fans alike, prompting discussions about preserving sportsmanship traditions in a post‑pandemic era.

Looking ahead, India’s victory reinforces its dominance in the Asian cricketing landscape and provides a morale boost ahead of the upcoming ICC World Cup and T20 World Cup cycles. For Pakistan, the narrow loss, coupled with Nawaz’s near‑century, signals a promising talent pool that could translate into future successes if nurtured effectively. The Asian Games experience also offers both boards valuable insights into managing high‑pressure encounters and the operational aspects of large‑scale tournaments. As the continent’s cricketing rivalry continues to evolve, fans can anticipate more electrifying clashes, with the added expectation that organizers will fine‑tune the event logistics to match the sport’s growing popularity.
